title: Marled scarf
subtitle: A scarf knitted with two yarn strands held together to create a tweedy colour blend.
excerpt: A scarf knitted flat with two contrasting yarn strands held together on 6 mm needles, finishing at 20 cm wide by 155 cm long. Holding two thinner yarns together as a single strand creates a marled or tweedy colour effect where both colours show throughout the fabric. Each strand is a DK-weight yarn; together they work at a bulky gauge.
sourceNotes: Knitting with two strands held together for texture and colour blending is documented in Victorian fancy knitting manuals including Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, under the terms 'double wool' and 'marled yarn'.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two or more strands of different-coloured yarn held together and worked as a single strand. The colours blend visually in the finished fabric, giving a tweedy or heathered effect.
Working two strands of yarn simultaneously as if they were one. Both strands pass through the stitch together on every knit and purl.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a scarf knitted flat with two DK-weight yarn strands
held together
on 6 mm needles, finishing at 20 cm wide and 155 cm long. The two strands together produce a
marled

fabric where both colours are visible throughout; the exact blend shifts subtly across the surface as the twist of the two strands varies. The pattern stitch is garter stitch (all knit, both sides) which keeps the fabric flat without blocking.

Garter stitch was chosen because the all-knit fabric is the simplest possible pattern for a beginner, and garter stitch lies flat without curling, which removes the need to block or add a border. The finished scarf needs about 230 m (approximately 80 g) each of two DK-weight yarn colours. Any two DK yarns of similar weight can be paired.
What you need

items.name: DK-weight yarn, colour A
items.substitutions: Any DK-weight yarn. For the most even marling, choose two yarns of similar thickness and twist.

items.name: 6 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 4 / US 10)

content.text: Gauge

14 sts x 18 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch with two DK strands held together on 6 mm needles, blocked. In garter stitch the row gauge is approximately 25 ridges per 10 cm (each ridge = 2 rows). One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by approximately 1.4 cm at this stitch count. Swatch with both specific yarns held together, as different DK yarns vary in thickness.
Pattern
Cast on
Wind colour A and colour B together into a single doubled strand (or work from both balls simultaneously). Use the
long-tail cast-on

with both strands held together to place 28 stitches on the needle. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 6 mm needles (circumference approximately 18.8 mm) and 28 stitches: (18.8 x 28) / 10 + 15 = 52.6 + 15 = about 68 cm. Leave at least 68 cm of both strands for the cast-on tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 28 stitches on the needle.
Body
Every row: K28 with both strands held together. (28 sts)
Repeat until the scarf measures 155 cm from the cast-on. At the halfway mark (approximately row 139 of 279 body rows), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 139 you should have 28 stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a standard bind-off with both strands held together. The garter stitch selvedge gives a naturally tidy cast-on and bind-off edge.
Common faults

One strand dropping out and being worked single. When both balls are running independently, one can slip behind the other and get missed for a stitch or two. Always keep both strands parallel and in the same path through the stitch. If you notice a dropped strand, rip back to the error before continuing.

Colour strands twisting into a spiral. Garter stitch worked flat naturally twists the two strands of a marled yarn together in one direction. Every 20 rows or so, let both balls drop and spin freely to untwist.
Gauge too tight with two DK strands on 6 mm needles. Some DK yarns are lighter than others. If your swatch is measuring tighter than 14 sts per 10 cm, move up to 6.5 mm or 7 mm needles.
Finishing

Weave in the cast-on and bind-off tails, keeping each colour strand in its own path along the wrong side. Garter stitch does not need blocking, but lightly pressing the scarf under a damp cloth settles the surface.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next
